title: Attention, cognitive load and forming meaning
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that school improvement is fundamentally about children learning more, better or faster, and that schools should therefore be built around how children learn. Using Willingham's simplified model of memory, he works through environment, working memory, encoding and retrieval, noting that attention is limited, that working memory is overloaded by self-regulation as well as content, and that meaning forms when new knowledge connects to what children already know. He questions the recent fetishisation of retrieval practice, asking whether pupils can retrieve what was never attended to or encoded. His key move is to apply the same model to adults: there is no improvement in children's learning at scale without organisational learning first, so leaders must direct colleagues' attention and reduce the cognitive load of teaching. He proposes a predictable annual sequence of collective focus (routines, relationships, attention and participation, performance, transition) and links it to Kennedy's persistent challenges of teaching as the backbone of professional development.
points: Hart treats the cognitive load of self-regulation, emotions and relationships as just as real as curriculum load, especially for young children.

Citing Graham Nuthall, he questions reliance on meticulously sequenced curricula, since pupils in one class hold starkly different prior knowledge, and suggests anchoring new learning in broader real-world concepts.
He argues the recent fetishisation of retrieval practice puts the cart before the horse, because material that was never attended to or encoded cannot be retrieved.

Willingham's model is applied to professional development: leaders should direct colleagues' attention to priorities and reduce the load of teaching, since organisational learning must precede improvement in pupils' learning.
He proposes a yearly cycle of collective focus (routines, relationships, attention and participation, performance, transition) and maps it onto Kennedy's persistent challenges of teaching.
quotes: The environment that children experience every day in their classrooms provides so much that they could pay attention to but attention has limited capacity. We have to work from the assumption that children can only learn about what they pay attention to and in a sea of curriculum-irrelevant stimuli, we have to prioritise supporting them to pay attention to the relevant stuff.

You only need to spend a few minutes with young children to know that their working memory capacity can easily be overloaded through attempts at self regulation, managing their emotions and navigating relationships with others. Reducing cognitive load is as much about supporting development in self regulation as it is about teaching the curriculum that goes way beyond the prime areas of learning in EYFS.

But as Graham Nuthall found, a class of children can have starkly different prior knowledge, despite our meticulously sequenced curriculum. How can we rely on every child having a secure foundation in previously taught concepts on which to build new learning?

Education is awash with advice on retrieval practice but can we retrieve what was not attended to, understood and encoded in the first place? The recent fetishisation of retrieval practice perhaps puts the cart before the horse.

There can be no improvement at scale of children’s learning without individual adults, teams and the organisation as a whole learning more first. Improvements in children’s attention, reduction in their cognitive load and multiple minds forming meaning rely on the adults doing something better or differently.

The beginning of the year demands that we focus on routines that can bring a feeling of predictability, security and maximise future learning time. When routines are established, we might shift our focus to further developing relationships with children.

Granted, we may need to slot in additional, necessary training at different points (ie safeguarding) but professional development can be much more than scheduled twilight INSET sessions. We’ll no doubt provide some formal training on each concept but we could also broker informal learning, iteratively refining shared understanding of the things that truly make a difference to school improvement.
